authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant

items.prompt: A validator scans n tokens once. Each opener is pushed once, and each matching closer pops one opener. What is the tightest offered worst-case time bound?
constraints: Reading and classifying one token takes Θ(1).
Each push, top check, match check, and pop takes Θ(1).

feedback.reason: The scan visits n tokens, and each token causes only constant work plus at most one matching push or pop.

blocks.text: Reading all n tokens already costs Θ(n). Each token performs constant branch work, every opener is pushed once, and no opener can be popped more than once because it leaves permanently when matched. The total is therefore Θ(n + pushes + pops) = Θ(n), matching the offered O(n) bound.

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: O(1) and O(log n) are too small because all n tokens must be inspected. O(n log n) and O(n²) are looser upper bounds, not the tightest offered bound; no sorting or repeated all-input scan occurs.

items.prompt: Select all statements that are sufficient components of the standard amortized argument for a one-pass candidate-stack scan.
constraints: The outer scan processes n input occurrences once.
Each push and pop takes Θ(1).

options.text: Each input occurrence is pushed at most once.
The inner pop loop performs n pops for every input occurrence.
Every occurrence must remain stored until the scan ends.
After an occurrence is popped, that same occurrence never returns to the stack.

feedback.reason: The aggregate bound follows from charging at most one push and one permanent pop to each input occurrence.

blocks.text: A single iteration may pop several candidates, but those pops consume distinct occurrences that cannot be popped again. Summed over the entire scan, there are at most n pushes and n pops, plus O(n) outer-loop work. This aggregate accounting yields O(n) total stack operations without claiming that each individual iteration is O(1).

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.inner_loop_n_each: That statement is the mistaken multiplication that produces O(n²); the same n candidates are not available to be popped on every iteration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.retain_all: Permanent retention is neither required nor true for a resolving candidate stack; removal is what makes the amortized charge finite.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.push_once: Without the one-push bound, an occurrence could re-enter repeatedly and the aggregate operation count would need a different proof.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.pop_once: Without permanent removal, the same occurrence could be charged multiple times and the linear aggregate bound would not follow.

items.prompt: One observed iteration of a candidate-stack scan pops k = 12 pending entries, and on other size-n inputs k can grow with n. Which complexity conclusion is justified when every entry is pushed once and popped at most once over the entire scan?

options.text: Any iteration with more than one pop makes the complete scan O(n²).
The iteration costs Θ(k), which can be Θ(n), but the whole scan remains Θ(n) in aggregate.
The expensive iteration should be called O(1) because each individual pop is O(1).
The loop must have removed and restored the same entry 12 times.

feedback.reason: Amortized analysis permits an expensive iteration when its work consumes operations that cannot recur for the same entries.

blocks.text: The observed 12 pops are 12 distinct constant-time operations. Asymptotically, the iteration costs Θ(k); because k can grow to n on another input, one iteration can be Θ(n). Each popped entry has nevertheless used its only pop. Across the whole scan, total pops are at most n, total pushes are at most n, and the outer scan costs Θ(n), so the aggregate is Θ(n).

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.total_quadratic: Multiple pops in one iteration do not imply n pops in every iteration; permanent removal prevents that repetition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.each_pop_constant_total: One pop is Θ(1), but k consecutive pops cost Θ(k). Treating k as an unbounded input-dependent count is what exposes a possible Θ(n) iteration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_entry_twelve_times: A popped entry leaves the stack; the iteration consumed 12 distinct pending entries.

items.prompt: A one-pass stack algorithm processes n input positions. Each position is pushed at most once and popped at most once. In the worst case, no position is popped until the end. What are the tightest offered worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds?
constraints: The per-position outer work and each stack operation take Θ(1).
Each retained position occupies Θ(1) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Bounded lifetime operations give O(n) total time, while an unresolved prefix may retain n entries at once.

blocks.text: The outer scan costs Θ(n), with at most n constant-time pushes and n constant-time pops, so total time is Θ(n). Space is a peak-state question: the stated legal input leaves all n constant-size position records pending simultaneously, establishing Θ(n) auxiliary space. The matching offered answers are O(n) time and O(n) space.

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: For time, O(1) and O(log n) cannot cover the mandatory n-position scan, while O(n log n) and O(n²) are loose. For space, O(1) and O(log n) cannot hold the stated n-entry frontier, while O(n log n) and O(n²) overstate the tight peak.

items.prompt: An editor commits n commands, storing one constant-size inverse record per command, and then performs n Undo operations. Each commit pushes once and each Undo pops once. What are the tightest offered total-time and maximum auxiliary-space bounds for history bookkeeping?
constraints: Each push, pop, and constant-size history-record operation takes Θ(1).
The cost of the document command itself is outside this bookkeeping question.

feedback.reason: There are 2n constant-time stack operations, and the history can hold n inverse records before Undo begins.

blocks.text: The history performs n constant-time pushes followed by n constant-time pops, so its total bookkeeping time is Θ(n + n) = Θ(n). Immediately before the first Undo, all n constant-size inverse records are retained, establishing Θ(n) peak auxiliary space. The matching offered answers are O(n) time and O(n) space.

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: O(1) and O(log n) are too small for 2n history operations or n simultaneous records. O(n log n) and O(n²) are loose rather than tight because no sorting, nested replay, or superlinear record size is included.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly reconciles “the stack does not always store every input item” with a worst-case O(n) space bound?

options.text: O(n) space means every input must retain every item until the end.
Removing any item at any time proves the worst-case space is O(1).
The bound becomes O(1) whenever equivalent state is stored in recursive frames.
Some inputs remove entries early; another legal input can leave all n entries pending.

feedback.reason: Worst-case space describes the largest legal peak occupancy, not mandatory occupancy on every input.

blocks.text: A resolving stack often shrinks, so actual occupancy can be far below n. Yet a monotone or otherwise non-resolving input can keep every candidate pending, producing a peak of n records. Both statements are therefore compatible: the stack is not a permanent archive by semantics, but its worst-case frontier size is linear.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_store_all: A Big-O upper bound does not claim equal occupancy for every input; it permits smaller states.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.space_is_constant: Occasional removal does not cap the maximum number of simultaneously pending records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_changes_bound: Recursive call frames also consume space, and syntax does not erase the state required by the algorithm.

items.prompt: A developer replaces a stack with a queue in a nested-structure validator. Both versions still perform O(n) container operations. Which review conclusion is correct?

options.text: Equal O(n) time proves the queue and stack versions are behaviorally equivalent.
The cost can remain O(n), but FIFO exposes the wrong unresolved opener.
Both linear versions remain incorrect unless recursive control flow supplies a call stack.
A queue is necessarily asymptotically faster because it removes from the front.

feedback.reason: Complexity is not a correctness proof; LIFO versus FIFO changes which unresolved state is inspected.

blocks.text: Both structures can support constant-time insertion and removal, yielding a linear count over n tokens. But nested validation requires the most recently opened unresolved delimiter, which a stack exposes and a queue does not. Replacing the structure can preserve Big-O notation while changing the algorithm's semantics. Recursion is optional if an explicit stack represents the required state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.equivalent_because_linear: Big-O suppresses ordering semantics; two linear algorithms can produce different answers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_required: An explicit stack is a complete iterative representation of the unresolved nesting state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.queue_is_faster: With appropriate implementations, both end operations can be O(1); the decisive difference here is order, not asymptotic speed.

items.prompt: Which accounting argument justifies O(n) total pop work when one iteration may pop many candidates?

options.text: Charge each item a constant credit when pushed; that credit pays for its one eventual pop, so all pushes and pops total O(n).
Assume every input iteration performs at most one pop because the code has one loop.
Ignore the while-loop cost because it is nested inside a linear scan.
Treat the stack as constant-size because it is a single container.

feedback.reason: Each concrete entry pays for at most one push and one pop, bounding total container operations even when costs cluster.

blocks.text: An individual iteration can pop Θ(n) entries, but those entries were previously pushed and cannot be popped again without a new push. Summing per-entry lifecycle events gives O(n) total time; maximum simultaneous stack size is a separate O(n) worst-case bound.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_pop_iteration: A single iteration can pop many entries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_inner: Nested loops require an aggregate argument, not syntax-based dismissal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stack_size_constant: A stack's container type does not bound its number of entries.

items.prompt: A monotonic stack algorithm pops dominated entries permanently. What does its auxiliary-space bound measure?

options.text: The maximum number of unresolved entries simultaneously retained, which can be O(n) even when many entries are eventually popped.
The total number of pushes, which is always O(1) because each entry is popped once.
The total number of pops; amortized O(n) time implies O(n) space automatically.
No auxiliary space exists because entries originated in the input.

feedback.reason: Space is peak live state, not cumulative operations or eventual retention after the scan.

blocks.text: A monotonic stack may retain a long increasing or decreasing prefix before any candidate is resolved. That peak can contain Θ(n) indices or records. Popping each entry once proves time, but it does not make the maximum simultaneous frontier constant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.total_pushes: Every input can be pushed once, so total pushes are O(n), not O(1), and cumulative work is not peak space.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.total_pops: Time and space measure different quantities.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.input_values_only: Stored indices, records, and stack metadata are auxiliary state even when values came from input.

items.prompt: A candidate-stack implementation has O(n) amortized time but returns the wrong nearest greater index after changing a strict comparison. What review conclusion follows?

options.text: The amortized cost argument may remain valid, but the monotonic invariant/output proof is broken and the implementation is not correct.
O(n) time proves the nearest answer because the stack still terminates.
Only space analysis needs revision; output differences are irrelevant to complexity review.
Replace the stack with a queue because any linear structure has the same result.

feedback.reason: Runtime and semantic correctness are separate claims; a finite amortized scan can still resolve the wrong candidates.

blocks.text: Changing < to <= can alter which equal candidates are popped and therefore which index is considered nearest or qualifying. The one-push/one-pop lifecycle may still establish O(n), but the comparator, stack-order invariant, and answer timing require a correctness review.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_proves_correct: Termination and asymptotic cost do not imply the returned indices satisfy the relation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.space_only_issue: Wrong output is a correctness defect independent of resource analysis.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.restore_queue: FIFO does not preserve the newest unresolved boundary relation that the stack uses.

items.prompt: Why can a monotonic-stack loop with an inner while still be O(n) amortized?

options.text: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so total stack operations are O(n).
The while loop necessarily makes every input pair compare.
The while loop does not remove elements, so its cost is zero.
The stack is O(n) because sorting dominates every loop.

feedback.reason: Amortized analysis charges each pop to the unique earlier push that created that entry.

blocks.text: Individual iterations can pop many items, but the total number of pushes and pops across the entire scan is linear.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nested_always_n2: Nested syntax alone does not prove quadratic total work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_pop: Popping is real work and is what the bound counts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_cost: A monotonic stack scan does not require sorting.

items.prompt: What controls auxiliary space in a stack-based nested-structure validator?

options.text: The maximum number of simultaneously unmatched opening structures.
The sum of all token values.
The square of the number of matching pairs.
Constant space regardless of nesting depth.

feedback.reason: The stack stores unresolved openings until their closers arrive.

blocks.text: A deeply nested input can leave O(n) tokens active even though each push and pop is O(1). Time and peak stack depth should be analyzed separately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.input_values_sum: Token magnitudes do not determine stored stack count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.total_pairs_squared: Each token is stored at most once in the active stack.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_always: Nesting depth can grow with input length.

items.prompt: What is the correctness bug if a monotonic-stack scan never flushes entries after the final input value?

options.text: Candidates with no later witness may remain unresolved instead of receiving the output sentinel.
The input is sorted unnecessarily at the end.
Every stack entry is pushed twice automatically.
The scan becomes constant time.

feedback.reason: End-of-input is the event that proves remaining candidates have no qualifying later value.

blocks.text: Initialize answers to the no-answer sentinel or pop/assign remaining entries in a final flush. Leaving work state in the stack is not a complete output.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.extra_sort: Flush logic does not sort data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_push: The bug is missing output assignment, not automatic duplicate insertion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_time: Unresolved entries still represent linear work or missing answers.

items.prompt: Which operation sequence preserves the standard LIFO invariant for processing a current token?

options.text: Inspect the top, pop resolved entries, then push the current unresolved state as required.
Read and modify the bottom for every token.
Remove any convenient stack entry that matches.
Push every token and never resolve prior state.

feedback.reason: The top is the only legal unresolved state to inspect or resolve in LIFO processing.

blocks.text: The exact order depends on the problem, but arbitrary removal or bottom access changes the data structure's semantics. Push and pop operations must preserve the stated invariant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bottom-only: Bottom access is not a constant-time LIFO top operation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random-remove: Removing below the top violates stack discipline.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.push-never-pop: Unresolved state would never receive answers.
